{{Quote|In five millennia, the Mandalorians fought with and against a thousand armies on a thousand worlds. They learned to speak as many languages and absorbed weapons technology and tactics from every war. And yet, despite the overwhelming influence of alien cultures, and the absence of a true homeworld and even species, their own language not only survived but changed little, their way of life and their philosophy remained untouched, and their ideals and sense of family, of identity, of nation, were only strengthened.|[[Mandalorians: Identity and Language]], published by the [[Galactic Institute of Anthropology]]|<ref name="TripleZero">''[[Republic Commando: Triple Zero]]''</ref>}}
'''''Mando'a''''', sometimes referred to simply as '''Mandalorian''', was the primary [[Language/Legends|language]] spoken by the [[Mandalorian/Legends|Mandalorian]] culture. Elements of ''Mando'a'' were taken from the language of the ancient [[Taung/Legends|Taungs]] of [[Coruscant/Legends|Coruscant]], from which the culture stemmed, evolving over [[Time/Legends|time]] to become something unique.

==Overview==
{{Quote|We don't have a word for hero. Being prepared to die for your family and friends, or what you hold dear, is a basic requirement for a ''Mando'', so it's not worth a separate word. It's only cowards we had to find a special name for.|[[Baltan Carid]]|<ref name="Revelation">''[[Legacy of the Force: Revelation]]''</ref>}}
The origins of ''Mando'a'' were believed to have lain with the [[Language/Legends|language]] of the [[Taung/Legends|Taungs]], an ancient race of [[Humanoid/Legends|Humanoid]] [[Primate/Legends|simians]] that originated on [[Coruscant/Legends|Coruscant]] in the [[Time/Legends|time]] [[Pre-Republic era|before]] the [[Galactic Republic/Legends|Galactic Republic]].<ref name="TMPaC" /> The Taungs were driven from Coruscant by the [[Human/Legends|Human]] [[Battalion/Legends|battalions]] of [[Zhell/Legends|Zhell]] after a lengthy war, and under the leadership of [[Mandalore the First/Legends|Mandalore the First]], conquered a new [[Planet/Legends|planet]] they named [[Mandalore/Legends|Mandalore]] in their leader's honor, becoming the first [[Mandalorian/Legends|Mandalorians]]—or ''Mando'ade'', "Children of Mandalore" in ''Mando'a''.<ref name="CSWE">''[[The Complete Star Wars Encyclopedia]]''</ref>

Despite this direct lineage, and the fact that the Taungs spoke an archaic dialect that evolved into the later ''Mando'a'',<ref name="GaW">''[[Galaxy at War]]''</ref> contemporary ''Mando'a'' contained unique elements unlike any found in other [[The galaxy/Legends|galactic]] languages. ''Mando'a'' had no grammatical cases, only two forms for a verb to take, a tense prefix system, and simplistic rules for forming adjectives from nouns and verb stems. Spelling and punctuation forms were optional, decided upon by the preference of the individual speaker—''jagyc'' and ''jagla'', for instance, were both correct ways of saying "masculine."<ref name="TMPaC" />

To understand and be able to speak ''Mando'a'' was one of the ''[[Resol'nare]]'', the six central tenets that an individual had to observe in their daily life should they wish to be a Mandalorian. This respect for the language, along with ''Mando'a''{{'s}} natural flexibility, meant that words drawn from other languages were a rarity,<ref name="TMPaC" /> and ''Mando'a'' changed very little throughout the centuries in spite of the many languages the Mandalorians learned to speak, and the vast influence from alien cultures.<ref name="TripleZero" />

If a new word for a thing or concept was needed, Mandalorians would typically draw upon the existing ''Mando'a'' vocabulary to form an appropriate term. ''Mando'a'' was an agglutinative language, meaning that many words were formed by combining two or more others, without changing their form, to create a new word with a new meaning.<ref name="TMPaC" /> An example of this was the term ''dar'jetii'', which is a combination of the ''Mando'a'' words ''dar'', meaning "no longer," and ''jetii'', the Mandalorian word for [[Jedi/Legends|Jedi]].

Literally translated, ''dar'jetii'' meant "no longer a Jedi," but was mostly used contextually to mean "[[Sith/Legends|Sith]]."<ref name="Mando'a">{{WebCite|url=http://www.karentraviss.com/page20/page26/index.html|text=Mando'a|work=[[Karen Traviss]]'s [https://karentraviss.com official website]|archivedate=20110925083955}}</ref> However, ''hut'tuun''—the Mandalorian word for "coward"—found its roots in the common Mandalorian dislike for [[Hutt/Legends|Hutts]], specifically their tendency to hire others to handle their martial needs in their stead.<ref name="TMPaC" />

[[Concordian/Legends|Concordian]], the language spoken on both the planet [[Concord Dawn/Legends|Concord Dawn]]<ref name="GttGAR">{{InsiderCite|84|Guide to the Grand Army of the Republic}}</ref> and Mandalore's [[Moon/Legends|moon]], [[Concordia/Legends|Concordia]],<ref name="The Mandalore Plot">{{TCW|The Mandalore Plot}}</ref> was a dialect of ''Mando'a''. As such, though they differed in certain aspects, the two languages were mutually intelligible, meaning that they were similar enough that an individual speaking one could easily converse with someone speaking the other.<ref name="O66" /> The [[Sasha ot Sulem's dialect|dialect]] spoken by the Human [[Youngling/Legends|child]] [[Sasha ot Sulem]] in [[3956 BBY]], following the girl's kidnapping and her time living among the Mandalorians on [[Dantooine/Legends|Dantooine]], was believed by the [[Jedi Knight/Legends|Jedi Knight]] [[Revan/Legends|Revan]] to be a jumbled offshoot of ''Mando'a''.<ref name="KotOR">''[[Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic]]''</ref>

==Grammar==
{{Quote|The language is a very regular. It has no cases; only two forms of the verb and a tense prefix system; and simple rules for creating adjectives out of nouns and verb stems. Spelling and punctuation have optional forms so it's hard to be completely ungrammatical.|[[Karen Traviss]] on Mando'a|<ref name="Mando'a" />}}
Word order indicates meaning, as in English.<ref name="Mando'a" />

''Mando'a'' was a primarily spoken language, rather than a written one, and was thus an expressive language that was often thought of as easy to learn, a trait highly desirable in a culture that regularly adopted adults from numerous races and species.

The language's grammar was relatively uncomplicated, but there were elements that necessitated adjustments for a speaker of [[Galactic Basic Standard/Legends|Basic]], including ''Mando'a''{{'s}} expression of tense, and its [[Gender/Legends|gender]]-neutrality.

Because Mandalorians believed in living their history, along with the idea that a tomorrow was not always a certainty, past and future tense were colloquially done away with.

Instead, the prefixes ''ru'' for "past," and ''ven'' for "future," were used in place of the more widely used tense forms.

There was also no passive verb form in ''Mando'a''; a verb was either active or simply absent from the statement.<ref name="TMPaC" />

'''Nouns'''

Nouns had no gender and ending vowels or consonants.<ref name="Mando'a" />

'''Plurals'''

When forming a plural, ''-e'' was added to the end of nouns ending in consonants, while ''-se'' was added to the end of nouns ending in a vowel.<ref name="TMPaC" />

As with most languages, there were exceptions to the rule, such as in the case of ''gett'' becoming ''gett'se''.<ref name="Mando'a" />

Originally, a plural was indicated with an ''-a'' suffix rather than an ''-e'', a practice that went away over time.<ref name="TMPaC" />

'''Verbs'''

Infinitive verbs ended in ''-ir'', ''-ar'', ''-ur'', ''-or'', or ''-er''. Removing the "r" at the end produced the stem.<ref name="TMPaC" />

''Ni vorer'' was incorrect, but ''Ni vore''—meaning "I accept" and using the inflected form—was correct.<ref name="Mando'a" />

Oftentimes, an apostrophe—known in ''Mando'a'' as a ''beten'', or "sigh"—was used to separate the terminal vowel, indicating the slight glottal pause of some Mandalorian accents.

Other uses for the ''beten'' were as an indication of a breath, for pronunciation, or a sign of a dropped letter or letters in a contraction. {{Quote|How do I tell Darman in Mandalorian that I love him?''"<br />"''Try...''ni kar'tayli gar darasuum.'' It's the same word as 'to know,' 'to hold in the heart,' ''kar'taylir''. But you add ''darasuum'', forever, and it becomes something rather different.|[[Etain Tur-Mukan]] and [[Bardan Jusik]]|<ref name="TripleZero" />}}
For instance, the sentence "I carry a saber" could be translated in ''Mando'a'' as the formal ''ni juri kad'', or the pronunciation-marked ''ni jur'i kad'', since the emphasis was placed on the second syllable in the word ''juri'', and even the more commonly contracted ''ni jur'kad''.

Dropping a terminal vowel when conjugating was quite common, especially in Mandalorian poetry and song.<ref name="TMPaC" />

Occasionally, certain verbs would be left out all together, and instead implied via word order. While this tendency to forgo certain words could be confusing to Basic speakers, and make the language appear abrupt, the militaristic Mandalorians had largely assumed the concise speech common in military orders. Whereas the literal translation for "It's good" would be ''bic cuyi jate'', a Mandalorian was much more likely to just say ''jate'', or "good," instead.<ref name="TMPaC" />

'''Gender and pronouns'''

Because ''Mando'a'' was a gender-neutral language, gender was implied by context.

''Buir'' meant both "mother" and "father," just as "son" and "daughter" were both represented by the word ''ad''. To specify gender, the adjectives of ''jagyc'' or ''dalyc''—male and female, respectively—could be added.

This grammatical system was a rarity for a language spoken by beings who [[Reproduction/Legends|reproduced]] sexually.<ref name="TMPaC" />

'''Interrogative (questions), imperative (commands), and negation'''

To form a question, the interrogative prefix ''tion'' was placed at the beginning of a sentence.

While ''Gar verborad'ni'' meant "You are hiring me," placing the ''tion'' prefix before ''gar'' would turn the statement into the question, ''Tion Gar verborad'ni?'': "Are you hiring me?"

Examples:

*''Tion gar gai?''<ref name="Mando'a" /> - What's your name?
*''Tion'ad''<ref name="Mando'a" /> - Who? (Lit: what person?)
*''Tion'ad hukaat'kama?''<ref name="Mando'a" /> - Who's watching your back?
*''Tion'cuy?''<ref name="Mando'a" /> - Who's that? (often used as a challenge to identify someone, like "Halt! Who goes there?")
*''Tion'jor''<ref name="Mando'a" /> - Why?
*''Tion'meh''<ref name="Mando'a" /> - What if?
*''Tion'solet?''<ref name="Mando'a" /> - How many? How much?
*''Tion'tuur''<ref name="Mando'a" /> - When? (lit. which day)

Another example of a meaningful prefix was ''ke'', also shortened to ''k'', which was drawn from the ''Mando'a'' word for "order," or ''ke'gyce'', and was placed at the start of a sentence to indicate a command. 

*''Ke narir haar'ke'gyce rol'eta resol!''<ref name="Mando'a" /> - Execute [[Order 66/Legends|Order 66]]!
*''Ke serim''<ref name="Mando'a" /> - Take aim!

In order to create the negative form in ''Mando'a'', the prefix ''n{{'}}'', ''nu'', ''nu{{'}}'', or ''ne'' was added before either the sentence or the individual word. ''Ne'briikase'' meant "unhappy," while ''Nu'ni juri kad'' meant "I don't carry a saber." The title of the song "[[Naasad'guur mhi – Mhi n'ulu]]" ("No one likes us - We don't care") has the negation on the verb ''ulur''.<ref name="Mando'a" />

''Naasad'' is not negation but a word meaning "none, not any"; it is similar to ''Dar'', meaning "gone, temporary, no longer," used in the words ''darasuum'' meaning "Eternity," ''dar'tome'' "seperated," and ''dar'buir''<ref name="Mando'a" /> "no longer a parent" (a legal term for parental divorce by child).

'''Adjectives and adverbs'''

Adjectives and adverbs were formed by adding the suffixes ''-la'' or ''-yc'' to the end of nouns. The inflections were:

*''-la'' or ''-yc'' (Example: Fast) (positive)
*''-shy'a'' (Example: Faster) (comparative)
*''-ne'' (Example: Fastest) (superlative)

The ''-la'' and ''-yc'' suffixes were interchangable; ''-shy'a'' and ''-ne'' had no other forms.<ref name="TMPaC" />

However, not all adjectives and adverbs contain ''-la'' or ''-yc''.

*''Di'kut'', meaning "idiot" in ''Mando'a'', could become ''di'kutla'', meaning "idiotic."<ref name="Mando'a" />

Comparatives and superlatives were formed in much the same way.

When creating a comparative, the suffix ''-shy'a'' was added to the standard adjective. For a superlative, the ''-ne'' suffix was added.

*Examples were the word ''dral'', meaning "bright," becoming ''dralshy'a'', or "brighter," and the word ''jate'', meaning "good," becoming ''jate'shya'', "better," and ''jatne'', "best."

''Mando'a'' made no distinction between adjectives and adverbs, and although a non-''Mando'a'' speaker might presume a Mandalorian to be uneducated should he say in Basic, "The boys done good," it was much more likely that they were simply unfamiliar with Basic's past tense and adverbial forms.

''Mando'a'' also made less use of articles such as "the" and "an" than Basic, generally adding them only for emphasis.<ref name="TMPaC" />

==Phonology and orthography==
''Mando'a'' had a similar pronunciation to Basic, with a few notable exceptions.

The letters "f," "x," or "z" were not used for ''Mando'a''{{'s}} own words, although the [[Mandalorian (writing system)/Legends|Mandalorian alphabet]] included the letters for greater ease in transliterating foreign words.<ref name="TMPaC" />

In the absence of the letter "f," ''Mando'a'' substituted the similar-sounding "''vh''" combination, and the Mandalorian "s" could be pronounced in the same way as a common "z." ''Ts'' was pronounced as "ts," "z" and "s" sounds.<ref name="Mando'a" />

Occasionally, the pronunciation of "d" was swapped with the more modern "t." ''Kote'' ("glory") could be pronounced KOH-day or KOH-tay.<ref>{{WebCite|url=http://www.karentraviss.com/html/grammarguide.htm|text=Mando'a - QUICK GRAMMAR GUIDE|work=[[Karen Traviss]]'s [https://karentraviss.com official website]|archivedate=20110713135503|nolive=1}}</ref><ref name="Mando'a" />

Certain Mandalorian communities still preferred to pronounce the letter "j" as in "fjord," instead of the more commonly heard hard "j" as in "joy."

When speaking, the first "h" in a word was typically aspirated—aside from its archaic form used in traditional songs and poems—and always pronounced when found in the middle of a word.

''Mando'a'' possessed no silent letters, though the opposite was often true of Mandalorian songs: terminal consonants could become extra syllables in order to better maintain rhythm and meter. For example, ''tor'' could easily become ''to-rah'', and ''tang'' could just as easily become ''tan-gah''.<ref name="TMPaC" /> ''kom'rk'' acquired an "o" sound - KOHM-or-rohk and ''kar'ta'' - kah-ROH-ta.<ref name="Mando'a" />

==Vocabulary==
{{Quote|The Mandalorian language has more terms of insult than any of the more widely spoken galactic tongues. But whereas most species choose insults that are based on parentage or appearance, the majority of Mandalorian pejoratives are concerned with cowardice, stupidity, laziness, dull conversation, or a lack of hygiene. It reveals the preoccupations of a nomadic warrior culture where bloodline matters less than personal qualities, faces are largely masked, and a clean, efficient camp is crucial to survival.|Mandalorians: Identity and Language, published by the Galactic Institute of Anthropology|<ref name="O66" />}}

==Written form==
{{Main|Mandalorian (writing system)/Legends}}
The Mandalorian alphabet consisted of twenty-six characters. The [[New Mandalorians/Legends|New Mandalorians]] used written Mandalorian quite frequently in their everyday lives. The [[True Mandalorians]] traditionally used it to provide information on personal datapads and ship-board display screens.

==Behind the scenes==
The first hints of a Mandalorian language was a [[Sasha ot Sulem's dialect|dialect]] that [[Revan/Legends|Revan]] learns from [[Sasha ot Sulem]] in the ''[[Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic]]'' video game. This was followed by Mandalorian words being used in the novel ''[[The Cestus Deception]]''. However, the creation of ''Mando'a'' as an individual language began with the introduction song to ''[[Star Wars: Republic Commando]]'', known as "[[Vode An]]" (Brothers All).

Sasha ot Sulem's language is a mix of Mandalorian and Galactic Basic Standard, and is therefore unrelated to this one. It is not known if it is a different canonical dialect or if it becomes non-canon.

''Mando'ade'' are a garrulous people, and [[Karen Traviss]] is British, and as such, the list above includes both obscenities and British slang.

Karen Traviss, though developing the majority of the language, has since removed all pages and documents concerning Mandalorian from her website. Development of the language has been left to the fans.

A glossary of many words and phrases is located in the back of Traviss's book ''[[Republic Commando: Triple Zero]]'' as well as in [[Star Wars Insider 86|''Star Wars Insider'' 86]]; other official language resources are online. For this article, an unofficial list has been culled from various Internet and literary sources.

Prior to 2002, a typeface consisting of narrow vertical characters was developed to represent the written form of the Mandalorian language. It was developed by [[Philip Metschan]] at the request of [[George Lucas]] to be used throughout [[Star Wars: Episode II Attack of the Clones|''Star Wars'': Episode II ''Attack of the Clones'']].<ref name="Portfolio">{{WebCite|url=http://www.principiagraphica.com/portfolio.htm|text=Philip Metschan's online portfolio|archivedate=20080718141854|nolive=1}}</ref><ref name="SWArchive-''Holographic'' Artist: Philip Metschan">{{SWArchive|url=episode-ii/feature/20020716/indexp2.html|text=''Holographic'' Artist: Philip Metschan}}</ref> This typeface, erroneously named "Mandelorian" by Metschan, can be seen on [[Jango Fett/Legends|Jango Fett's]] [[Slave I/Legends|''Slave I'']] ship-board display screens throughout the film. The full official typeface can be seen on his website.<ref>{{WebCite|url=http://www.metschanmedia.com/philip_metschan//portfolio.htm|text=Star Wars Typefaces|work=Philip Metschan's portfolio|nobackup=1}}</ref>
